```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# The ragg device writes smaller figure files; without it the default is used.
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png")
options(bayesEfron.use_cli = FALSE, width = 80)
has_metafor <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)
num <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
```

This vignette shows how to pass estimates and standard errors to
`bayes_efron_fit()` from a data frame, from metafor or as two vectors. It
also shows where the site labels appear in the results, and how to compare
a fit with the normal random-effects model from metafor.

```{r library}
library(bayesEfron)
```

The model needs two numbers for each site: an estimate of the effect and
the standard error of that estimate. Data rarely arrive in that form. A
table may have variances where standard errors are wanted, or the estimates
may still have to be computed from the means, standard deviations and
sample sizes of two groups. The sites (studies, firms, schools) usually
have names as well, which you will want to see again beside the results.
`as_bef_data()` handles the first case and, together with
`metafor::escalc()`, the second, and a fit keeps the names.

## Estimates in a data frame

We start with the callback data from `vignette("bayesEfron")`, which have
one row for each of 97 firms.

```{r data}
head(krw_discrimination[, c("firm_name", "yi", "vi", "sei")], 4)
```

`yi` is the difference between the callback probabilities of
applications with distinctively white and distinctively Black names at
the firm, `vi` its sampling variance and `sei` its standard error. The
function `as_bef_data()` finds the two columns that it needs by their
names, and its `site` argument names the column that contains the labels:

```{r by-name}
dat <- as_bef_data(krw_discrimination, site = "firm_name")
dat
```

It takes the first of these names that the data frame has, here `yi` and
`sei`:

- estimates: `theta_hat`, `yi`, `estimate`, `effect`, `y`;
- standard errors: `sigma`, `se`, `std_error`, `stderr`, `sei`.

If your columns have other names, give them in the arguments `theta_hat`
and `sigma`. If the second column contains variances, as `vi` does, set
`variance = TRUE` and the function takes the square roots.

```{r variance}
from_variances <- as_bef_data(krw_discrimination, sigma = "vi",
                              variance = TRUE, site = "firm_name")
all.equal(from_variances$sigma, dat$sigma)
```

```{r data-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(nrow(krw_discrimination) == 97L,
          isTRUE(all.equal(krw_discrimination$vi, krw_discrimination$sei^2)),
          identical(dat$names, krw_discrimination$firm_name),
          identical(dat$source, "data.frame"),
          is.null(as_bef_data(krw_discrimination)$names),
          inherits(try(as_bef_data(krw_discrimination[1:4, ]), silent = TRUE),
                   "try-error"),
          inherits(try(as_bef_data(krw_discrimination[c(1, 1:5), ],
                                   site = "firm_name"), silent = TRUE),
                   "try-error"),
          # A column of variances given as standard errors draws a warning.
          inherits(tryCatch(as_bef_data(krw_discrimination, sigma = "vi"),
                            warning = function(w) w), "warning"),
          !inherits(tryCatch(as_bef_data(transform(krw_discrimination, spread = vi),
                                         sigma = "spread"),
                             warning = function(w) w), "warning"))
```

`as_bef_data()` warns when a column with a name that begins with `vi` or
`var` is given as the standard errors without `variance = TRUE`. It cannot
detect variances under another name, because both are positive numbers, so
check the range of `sigma` in the printed object.

The function throws an error if a value is missing, if a standard error is
not positive, if a label occurs twice or if there are fewer than 5 sites.
It does not drop incomplete rows, because the number of sites would then
change without notice. For example, a missing standard error gives this
error:

```{r missing}
incomplete <- krw_discrimination
incomplete$sei[3] <- NA
try(as_bef_data(incomplete))
```

We can pass `dat` to `bayes_efron_fit()` as it is.

```{r fit-call, eval = FALSE}
fit <- bayes_efron_fit(dat, seed = 20250807)
```

You can also pass the data frame itself when its columns have the names
listed above. Its row names, if they have been set, are then the labels.

## Group summaries and metafor

Often the estimates have not been computed yet, and each study reports the
mean, the standard deviation and the size of two groups. From such
summaries, `metafor::escalc()` computes an estimate and its sampling
variance [@viechtbauer2010], and `as_bef_data()` accepts its result.

As an example we apply `escalc()` to the 9 studies that @normand1999
analyzed, which compare the length of hospital stay of stroke patients
under specialized and under routine care. The data are in the metadat
package, which metafor loads.

```{r escalc, eval = has_metafor, message = FALSE}
library(metafor)
stroke <- escalc(
  measure = "MD",
  m1i = m1i, sd1i = sd1i, n1i = n1i,
  m2i = m2i, sd2i = sd2i, n2i = n2i,
  data = dat.normand1999, slab = source
)
stroke[, c("source", "m1i", "m2i", "yi", "vi")]
```

We set `measure = "MD"`, so the estimate `yi` is the difference between
the two means, here in days, and `vi` is the sum of the two squared
standard errors of the means, $s_1^2 / n_1 + s_2^2 / n_2$. A difference in
the original units is the natural choice when every study measures the
outcome in the same way, as these do. When the studies use different
instruments, as the teacher expectancy studies in
`vignette("teacher-expectancy")` did with their IQ tests, the standardized
mean difference (`measure = "SMD"`) puts the estimates on a common scale.

From an `escalc` object, `as_bef_data()` takes the column `yi` as the
estimates and the square roots of `vi` as the standard errors.

```{r escalc-convert, eval = has_metafor}
stroke_dat <- as_bef_data(stroke)
as.data.frame(stroke_dat)
```

```{r escalc-facts, include = FALSE, eval = has_metafor}
unlabeled <- stroke
attr(unlabeled$yi, "slab") <- NULL
by_row <- unlabeled
rownames(by_row) <- paste("study", 1:9)
stopifnot(nrow(stroke) == 9L,
          identical(stroke_dat$names, as.character(dat.normand1999$source)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(stroke_dat$sigma, sqrt(as.numeric(stroke$vi)))),
          is.null(as_bef_data(unlabeled)$names),
          identical(as_bef_data(by_row)$names, paste("study", 1:9)))
```

The labels are the ones given to `escalc()` in its `slab` argument. Without
`slab`, row names that have been set are used.

Although 9 studies are enough for the function to run, we can learn little
from them about the shape of the distribution of effects. With so few
sites, the result depends strongly on the range of the grid, as
`vignette("teacher-expectancy")` shows for 19 studies.

## Two vectors

If your estimates and standard errors are two vectors, pass them to
`bayes_efron_fit()` as its first two arguments. The names of the estimates,
if they have any, become the labels. To have the two vectors checked before
running a fit, give them to `as_bef_data()` as a list, in which an element
`names` can supply the labels:

```{r list}
as_bef_data(list(
  theta_hat = krw_discrimination$yi,
  sigma = krw_discrimination$sei,
  names = krw_discrimination$firm_name
))
```

Whatever the form, the estimates should be the original ones. Estimates
that have already been shrunk, such as the posterior means from another
model, are not independent noisy observations of the effects, and passing
them as if they were changes the model.

## Site labels in the results

A fit stores the site labels. To show this we use `krw_fit`, the fit of
the callback data that comes with the package, made with the
`bayes_efron_fit()` call above and `thin = 15`. Its table of site effects
has the labels in the column `label`.

```{r labels}
fit <- krw_fit
head(site_summary(fit)[, c("site", "label", "estimate", "mean", "lower",
                           "upper")], 4)
```

You can choose a site by its label wherever a function takes `sites`, and
the returned vectors are named by label. Here we pick four firms and
print, for each, the probability of a positive gap and the posterior mean
in percentage points:

```{r by-label}
chosen <- c("Rite Aid", "KFC", "Safeway", "Genuine Parts (Napa Auto)")
round(exceedance_prob(fit, sites = chosen), 3)
round(100 * coef(fit)[chosen], 2)
```

```{r label-facts, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(site_summary(fit)$label, krw_discrimination$firm_name),
          identical(names(coef(fit)), krw_discrimination$firm_name),
          identical(names(exceedance_prob(fit, sites = chosen)), chosen),
          identical(site_summary(fit, sites = "Safeway")$site,
                    which(krw_discrimination$firm_name == "Safeway")),
          isTRUE(all.equal(site_summary(fit)$estimate, krw_discrimination$yi)))
```

The plots show the labels as well, here for the same four firms.

```{r label-plot, fig.height = 2.6, fig.alt = "Posterior means and intervals of the callback gaps of four firms chosen by name, each row labeled with the name of the firm."}
plot_sites(fit, sites = chosen, scale = 100)
```

Without labels a site is identified by its number, which is its position
in the input, so keep the rows of your data in the order in which they
were fitted. If the sites have labels, that order no longer matters for
finding a site.

## Comparison with the normal model from metafor

A metafor user will want to see the result next to the normal
random-effects model. We plot the estimated distribution of effects with
`plot_g()`, and `normal = TRUE` adds that model: a normal distribution with
its mean and standard deviation estimated from the same estimates by
restricted maximum likelihood (REML).

```{r normal-plot, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "The estimated density of the callback gaps in percentage points with its 90 percent band, and the dashed curve of a normal distribution fitted by REML."}
plot_g(fit, normal = TRUE, scale = 100)
```

The dashed curve leaves out the uncertainty of its two parameters, whereas
the band around the solid curve is a posterior interval. See
`vignette("bayesEfron")` for what we can conclude about the callback gaps
from the two curves.

The same two numbers come from `metafor::rma()` once its iteration is
allowed to run to convergence, here with a smaller `threshold`:

```{r rma, eval = has_metafor}
loose <- rma(yi, vi, data = krw_discrimination, method = "REML")
tight <- rma(yi, vi, data = krw_discrimination, method = "REML",
             control = list(threshold = 1e-10))
rbind(default = c(mean = coef(loose)[[1]], sd = sqrt(loose$tau2)),
      tightened = c(mean = coef(tight)[[1]], sd = sqrt(tight$tau2)))
```

```{r rma-facts, include = FALSE, eval = has_metafor}
# The normal curve that plot_g() draws: its standard deviation follows from
# the height of its peak.
curve <- ggplot2::layer_data(plot_g(fit, normal = TRUE), 2L)
curve <- curve[curve$linetype == "dashed", ]
drawn_sd <- 1 / (sqrt(2 * pi) * max(curve$y))
off <- abs(sqrt(loose$tau2) - sqrt(tight$tau2)) / sqrt(tight$tau2)
studies <- rma(yi, vi, data = raudenbush1985, method = "REML")
studies_tight <- rma(yi, vi, data = raudenbush1985, method = "REML",
                     control = list(threshold = 1e-10))
stopifnot(abs(drawn_sd - sqrt(tight$tau2)) / sqrt(tight$tau2) < 1e-3,
          off > 0.003, off < 0.005,
          tight$tau2 > 0.0002, tight$tau2 < 0.00025,
          abs(sqrt(studies$tau2) - sqrt(studies_tight$tau2)) /
            sqrt(studies_tight$tau2) < 0.001)
print(c(drawn_sd, sqrt(tight$tau2), off))
```

By default `rma()` stops when its estimate of the variance of the effects
changes by less than $10^{-5}$ from one step to the next. That is early
for estimates on a small scale. The variance of these gaps is about
0.0002, and the default leaves the standard deviation 0.4% away from the
value at convergence, which is the value that `plot_g()` shows. To plot a
normal model fitted in another way, give its two numbers as
`normal = c(mean = ..., sd = ...)`.
